The Simple Project Break-Even Year is the first year in which the aggregated savings are greater than or equal to all aggregated investments, without considering tax incentives such as the ITC or MACRS.

The Detailed Project Break-Even Year is the first year in which the aggregated savings are greater than or equal to all aggregated investments, and includes tax incentives such as the ITC or MACRS when computing the Break-Even Year.

The Simple Project Payback Period is calculated using the upfront investments in the first year and average annual savings. This value does not consider re-investments (for equipment replacement at end of lifetime). It also does not include tax incentives such as the ITC or MACRS.

Definition of Detailed Project Payback Period

In Xendee, the Payback Period is a financial metric that estimates how long it will take for an investment to recover its total cost including replacement costs and accounting for tax incentives through generated cash inflows or savings. It represents the point at which a project has fully returned its upfront and ongoing investment.

This measure focuses only on the period up to payback and does not consider cash flows that occur after the investment is recovered. Because of this, it is widely used as a risk indicator: projects that reach payback sooner are typically viewed as less risky, since short-term forecasts are generally more reliable than long-term ones.

Calculation:

The Payback Period is calculated using the following formula:

Payback Period = A + (B / C)

In this formula, A represents the last year in which the cumulative non-discounted cash flow remains negative, indicating the final year before the project recovers its full investment.

B is the absolute value of the cumulative cash flow at the end of year A. This value shows how much of the initial investment remains to be recovered at that point in time.

C represents the cash inflow in the period immediately following year A. This is the amount of savings or revenue generated in the next year that contributes toward recovering the remaining investment.

Cumulative cash flow is defined as total inflows to date minus the initial investment, adjusted for replacement costs and tax incentives.

The Payback Period value directly corresponds to the last year in the detailed savings cash flow table that still shows a negative cumulative non-discounted cash flow, making it easy to trace the result back to the cash flow details.

Detailed Payback Period is reported as undefined if the last year with a negative cumulative cash flow is the final year reported in the cash flow table.

HelpText: XENDEE Project Savings to Investment Ratio
<KEYVALUE>: The XENDEE Project Savings to Investment Ratio considers all aggregated investments and average annual savings over the number of reporting years (Equipment Lifetime Financing) or over the project length (Loan Term Financing).

Return on Investments is the total return of the project divided by the upfront costs (including reinvestments). The year-over-year ROI uses the cumulative net profit (or loss) and cumulative costs through the year being calculated.

The total operational costs for the reference case. This includes energy, fuel, maintenance, CO2, load shedding, and incoming PPA costs, less energy sales and incentives. Note: for user-defined reference values, OPEX is assumed to be the reference cost.

The total operational costs as calculated in the optimized case. This includes energy costs, fuel, maintenance, CO2 charges, load shedding costs, and incoming PPA costs less energy sales and other non-tax driven incentives.

The percent reduction in operating costs when using the optimized system compared to a baseline (reference case). These savings usually come from investing in better equipment or running the system more efficiently.

This value represents the total worth of the expected savings over the project lifetime, expressed in thousands of {CURRENCY_NAME_PLURAL_LOWERCASE} (k{CURRENCY_SYMBOL}). It is calculated by discounting future cashflows from the project - specifically the savings recorded in the Cashflow Table: Savings - to account for the time value of money. A positive NPV indicates that the project is expected to generate more savings than it costs, making it financially beneficial. A negative NPV suggests the opposite. The NPV is presented in thousands of dollars (k$) for clarity and ease of comparison.

The IRR shows the expected return of the project by identifying the discount rate that brings the Net Present Value (NPV) to zero over its lifetime. If the project has no service agreements, it is based on net annual cash flows. If it includes service agreements, it is based on the developers annual costs. IRR helps compare the profitability of different project options.

Definition of Generation-Based Levelized Cost of Electricity

Generation-Based Levelized Cost of Electricity (Gen-Based LCOE) is the average cost per kWh of electricity generated by the system over its lifetime, discounted to present value.

Gen-Based LCOE = Net Present Cost / (Net Present Purchased Electricity + Net Present Generated Electricity), both adjusted to present value if multiyear analyses are used.

Net Present Cost: Total of all lifetime system costs (equipment, operations, maintenance), adjusted to present day value.

Note: Revenue from Energy as a Service (EaaS) and Charging as a Service (CaaS) is not included.

Net Present Purchased Electricity: The total amount of electricity bought from the grid, adjusted to present day value.

Net Present Generated Electricity: The total electricity produced by the system, also adjusted to present day value.

Definition of Load-Served Levelized Cost of Electricity

Load-Served Levelized Cost of Electricity (Load-Served LCOE) is the average cost per kWh of electricity supplied by the system over its lifetime, discounted to present value.

Load-Served LCOE = Net Present Cost / Net Present Electrical Load Served, both adjusted to present value.

Net Present Cost: All costs to build and operate the system (equipment, operations, maintenance), adjusted to present value.

Note: Revenue from Energy as a Service (EaaS) and Charging as a Service (CaaS) is not included.

Net Present Electrical Load Served: The total electricity delivered to meet on-site demand, adjusted to present value. Usually, this reflects the original energy needs of the site (excluding any curtailed load).

The Savings cashflow table below displays the savings the system produces relative to the reference. The lines shown are the savings that the solution creates.

A positive value is a savings while a negative is a loss. The sum of the individual savings terms is used to calculate the net present value of the system.

The cost cashflow table below displays the costs to run the system, not relative to any reference. The lines shown are the costs that the solution is subject to.

A positive value is a revenue while a negative is a cost. The sum of the individual cost terms is used to calculate the system net present costs.

Definition of Levelized Cost of Charging

Levelized Cost of Charging (LCOC) is the average cost per kWh of electricity supplied to the EV fleet by the system over the project term. It represents the price per kWh that the system would need to receive to break even over its lifetime. This is calculated using the formula:

LCOC = Net Present Cost / Net Present EV Demand Met

Net Present Cost: This is the sum of all costs over the lifetime of the system, discounted to present value. It includes capital expenditures (CAPEX), operational expenses (OPEX), and maintenance costs. These costs are offset by any financial incentives such as subsidies, tax benefits, or revenue from programs like Demand Response and electricity export sales. Revenue from Energy as a Service and Charging as a Service are excluded and do not offset the costs.

Net Present EV Demand Met: This is the total EV fleet demand served by the microgrid, discounted to the present value. This is typically the original EV fleet demand of the system (less any curtailed load).

The LCOC is the $/kWh cost for the developer to provide EV charging on-site at the microgrid - it is used to calculate the CaaS rate that will incur sufficient revenue to both recover installation and O&M costs and return a profit. Note that LCOC does not include EV sales revenue and only represents the cost to the developer.
